Clinical Pathology

Clinical pathology - laboratory diagnostics, hematology, urinalysis, blood transfusion - nursing care and interpretation.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe common clinical pathology tests
  • Explain nursing care for blood transfusion
  • State patient teaching for laboratory tests

In simple terms

Clinical pathology involves laboratory testing of blood, urine, and other body fluids to diagnose disease. Nurses collect specimens, prepare patients for tests, and interpret results to guide patient care.

Common clinical pathology tests

Test Purpose Key findings
Complete blood count (CBC) Blood cell counts Anemia, infection, bleeding disorders
Blood glucose Blood glucose level Diabetes diagnosis and monitoring
Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) Kidney function Kidney dysfunction
Serum creatinine Kidney function Kidney dysfunction
Liver function tests (LFTs) Liver function Liver damage, hepatitis
Coagulation profile Blood clotting Bleeding disorders, anticoagulant monitoring
Blood gases Oxygen, carbon dioxide, pH Respiratory and metabolic disorders

Blood transfusion

Component Indication Administration
Packed red blood cells Anemia, blood loss IV infusion, monitor for reaction
Fresh frozen plasma Clotting factor deficiency IV infusion, monitor for reaction
Platelets Thrombocytopenia IV infusion, monitor for reaction
Cryoprecipitate Fibrinogen deficiency IV infusion, monitor for reaction

Nursing care

  • Specimen collection - collect blood, urine, stool, sputum specimens correctly; label accurately; send promptly to laboratory
  • Blood transfusion - two identifiers; check blood group/cross-match; start slowly (15 minutes); stay with patient first 15 minutes; monitor vitals
  • Transfusion reaction - fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, back pain, dark urine; STOP transfusion, inform doctor, keep IV open with normal saline, save bag and tubing
  • Patient teaching - explain test purpose, preparation requirements, what to expect during procedure

🔴 Transfusion reaction

Stop transfusion at the first sign of reaction (fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, back pain, dark urine); inform doctor; keep IV line open with normal saline; save bag and tubing.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Specimen collection - collect blood, urine, stool, sputum specimens correctly; label accurately; send promptly to laboratory
  • Blood transfusion - two identifiers; verify blood group/cross-match; start slow (15 min); stay with patient first 15 minutes; monitor vitals
  • Transfusion reaction - fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, back pain, dark urine; STOP transfusion, inform doctor, keep IV open with normal saline, save bag and tubing
  • Patient teaching - explain test purpose, preparation requirements, what to expect during procedure
  • Laboratory values - interpret common laboratory results; report abnormal results to healthcare provider

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Common blood tests: CBC, blood glucose, BUN, serum creatinine, LFTs, coagulation profile, blood gases.
  2. Blood transfusion: two identifiers; check blood group/cross-match; start slowly (15 minutes); stay with patient first 15 minutes; monitor vitals.
  3. Transfusion reaction: fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, back pain, dark urine; STOP transfusion, inform doctor, keep IV open with normal saline, save bag and tubing.
  4. Specimen collection: collect blood, urine, stool, sputum correctly; label accurately; send promptly to laboratory.
  5. Patient teaching: explain test purpose, preparation requirements, what to expect during procedure.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. CBC: hemoglobin, hematocrit, white blood cell count, platelet count - assess for anemia, infection, bleeding disorders.
  2. Blood glucose: fasting and random; diagnose and monitor diabetes.
  3. BUN and creatinine: kidney function; elevated levels indicate kidney dysfunction.
  4. LFTs: ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin; assess liver function.
  5. Coagulation profile: PT, INR, aPTT; assess clotting function; monitor warfarin therapy.

📌 Memory trick

Transfusion reaction: STOP - Stop transfusion, Tell doctor, Open IV line with normal saline, Preserve bag and tubing.

60-second revision

  • Clinical pathology: laboratory testing of blood, urine, and body fluids.
  • Common tests: CBC, blood glucose, BUN, creatinine, LFTs, coagulation profile, blood gases.
  • Blood transfusion: two identifiers; start slowly; monitor vitals; stay with patient first 15 minutes.
  • Transfusion reaction: fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, back pain, dark urine; STOP transfusion, inform doctor, save bag.
  • Patient teaching: explain test purpose, preparation, what to expect.

Test yourself

CBC stands for:

Answer: A. CBC = complete blood count; measures red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, hemoglobin, hematocrit.

Blood transfusion reaction signs include:

Answer: A. Transfusion reaction signs: fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, back pain, dark urine; STOP transfusion, inform doctor, keep IV open with normal saline, save bag and tubing.

Blood transfusion should be started:

Answer: B. Blood transfusion should be started slowly (15 minutes) and the nurse should stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes to monitor for reaction.

Blood specimen should be:

Answer: B. Blood specimen should be collected with correct patient identifiers (name and ID band); label accurately; send promptly to laboratory.

Blood glucose monitoring is used for:

Answer: A. Blood glucose monitoring is used for diabetes diagnosis and monitoring; fasting and random blood glucose tests.
